content_voiceover: This table is the genotype to phenotype ladder for alpha thalassemia, and you need to know it cold. With four functional alpha genes you're normal. Lose one gene, that's silent carrier, with a completely normal hemoglobin and MCV, so it's truly silent on routine labs. Lose two genes, either in cis as alpha-thal-1 or in trans as alpha-thal-2, and you get thalassemia trait: mild microcytic anemia, hemoglobin around twelve to thirteen, MCV seventy to eighty, essentially the phenocopy of iron deficiency that trips people up on boards. Lose three genes and you get hemoglobin H disease, with five to thirty percent Hb H, which is a beta-4 tetramer, hemoglobin dropping to six to ten, and MCV down to sixty to seventy; this is clinically significant hemolytic anemia. Lose all four genes and it's hydrops fetalis, essentially incompatible with life, hemoglobin Barts near ninety percent, a gamma-4 tetramer with such high oxygen affinity it can't deliver oxygen to tissues, fatal in utero or at birth. The Taiwan-specific numbers matter too: alpha thalassemia affects three to five percent of Taiwanese, with alpha-thal-1 around five percent and alpha-thal-2 one to three percent, and the severe non-deletional HbH genotype, minus minus over alpha-CS-alpha, is a big test point because it behaves more severely than the deletional forms despite starting with the same number of functioning genes.
keypoints: 4 genes lost = hydrops fetalis (Hb Barts gamma4 ~90%, fatal)
3 genes lost = HbH disease (HbH beta4 5-30%, Hb 6-10, MCV 60-70)
2 genes lost = thalassemia trait (mimics iron deficiency, MCV 70-80)
Non-deletional HbH (--/alphaCSalpha) is clinically more severe than deletional
keypoint_voiceover: Key numbers to lock in: losing all four alpha genes causes hydrops fetalis, with Hb Barts, a gamma-4 tetramer, near ninety percent, and it's fatal in utero or at birth. Losing three genes gives hemoglobin H disease, a beta-4 tetramer, with hemoglobin six to ten and MCV sixty to seventy. Losing two genes gives thalassemia trait, which mimics iron deficiency with an MCV of seventy to eighty. Losing just one gene is the silent carrier state, with entirely normal labs. And remember the exam trap: non-deletional hemoglobin H disease, genotype minus minus over alpha Constant-Spring alpha, runs a more severe clinical course than the deletional forms.
